title: The Ugly Stepsister
author: VirtueVigil Editorial Team
cast: Thea Sofie Loch Naess as Agnes/Cinderella
studio: Mer Film / Lava Films / Motor / Zentropa

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: NOT A WOKE TRAP. The Ugly Stepsister is marketed exactly as what it is: a body horror feminist retelling of Cinderella from the stepsister's perspective. The trailer, festival coverage, and critical reception all telegraph the film's themes of beauty standards, patriarchal violence, and female liberation. Conservative viewers who walk in expecting a conventional fairy tale retelling are not paying attention to the marketing. The film does not disguise its feminist thesis behind genre packaging. It wears it on its mutilated sleeve from minute one.

director.name: Emilie Blichfeldt
director.ideology: PROGRESSIVE FEMINIST. Blichfeldt conceived the film from her own struggles with body image and explicitly intended to 'provoke both empathy and discomfort and inspire the audience to reflect upon their perceptions of, and relationship to, beauty.' Her cinematic influences include David Cronenberg, Julia Ducournau (Raw), and Dario Argento. She uses body horror as a feminist tool to critique the violence women inflict on themselves in pursuit of patriarchal beauty standards.
director.profile: Emilie Blichfeldt is a Norwegian filmmaker who made her feature directorial debut with The Ugly Stepsister. She developed the film while working on her thesis project at the Norwegian Film School. The project began as a story about a woman with a 'talking vulva that tells her she's lonely' before evolving into a Cinderella reimagining based on the Brothers Grimm's 'Aschenputtel.' Blichfeldt's body horror approach was inspired by a deep dive into David Cronenberg's filmography after watching Crash (1996) in 2015, along with the work of Italian directors Dario Argento and Lucio Fulci. Julia Ducournau's Raw (2016) was a direct influence on using body horror as feminist commentary. The film premiered at the 2025 Sundance Film Festival and screened at the 75th Berlin International Film Festival before its US release through IFC Films.

writer.name: Emilie Blichfeldt
writer.profile: Blichfeldt wrote the screenplay herself, drawing from the Brothers Grimm's 'Aschenputtel' (their darker version of Cinderella, which includes the stepsisters cutting off parts of their feet to fit the glass slipper). She reimagined the fairy tale entirely from Elvira's perspective, transforming the 'ugly stepsister' from a villain into a sympathetic victim of a patriarchal beauty machine. The script layers body horror over fairy tale structure to create a sustained metaphor for the real-world violence of beauty culture.

lead_producer.name: Maria Ekerhovd
lead_producer.company: Mer Film (Norway) / Lava Films / Motor / Zentropa

composer.name: Kaada (John Erik Kaada) and Vilde Tuv
composer.profile: Kaada is a Norwegian experimental musician known for atmospheric and unsettling compositions. Vilde Tuv is a Norwegian folk musician. Together, their score blends fairy tale whimsy with horror textures, mirroring the film's tonal blend of dark humor and grotesque violence.

fidelityCasting.assessment: The Ugly Stepsister is based on the Brothers Grimm version of Cinderella ('Aschenputtel'), which is significantly darker than the Disney adaptation most audiences know. In the Grimm version, the stepsisters cut off parts of their feet to fit the glass slipper, and birds peck out their eyes at the wedding. Blichfeldt's film takes this darkness and amplifies it exponentially. The key adaptation choice is perspective. Traditional Cinderella stories center the beautiful, virtuous heroine and treat the stepsisters as comic villains deserving punishment. Blichfeldt flips this entirely, making Elvira the sympathetic protagonist and revealing Cinderella/Agnes as just another player in the same rigged beauty game. This is a deliberate feminist inversion of the source material. The fairy tale structure is preserved - ball, prince, glass slipper, midnight deadline - but the moral framework is completely rewritten. The Grimm tale punished vanity and rewarded virtue (defined as beauty plus kindness). Blichfeldt's version argues that the entire system - the beauty standards, the marriage market, the mother's cruelty - is the villain. Prince Julian is depicted as a shallow womanizer rather than a worthy prize, which directly subverts the fairy tale's premise. Whether this represents creative enrichment or ideological hijacking depends on your view of adaptation. The film is honest about what it is doing. It is a feminist deconstruction, not a faithful retelling. The casting is all-Norwegian and Scandinavian, appropriate for a Norwegian production. There is no diversity casting controversy.

parentalGuidance.mpaaDescriptors: Strong bloody violence, disturbing body horror imagery, nudity, sexual content
contentWarnings: Extensive body horror: eyelashes sewn into eyelids, crude cosmetic surgeries, foot mutilation with a butcher knife
A mother sedates her daughter and mutilates her foot to fit a glass slipper
A giant tapeworm is ingested for weight loss and later expelled through the mouth in graphic detail
A rotting corpse is stored in the house and shown decomposing over the course of the film
Sexual content: a character is shown having sex with a stable boy; the stepmother performs a sexual act on a nobleman
Vomiting, hair loss, and visible malnutrition from the tapeworm
Blood and gore throughout, particularly in the cosmetic surgery and foot-cutting sequences
Psychological abuse: a mother systematically destroys her daughter's body and self-worth in pursuit of a marriage alliance
A character falls down stairs, breaking her nose and chipping teeth
Themes of self-mutilation, eating disorders, and body dysmorphia presented through fairy tale allegory
A vision of a dead mother appears to a sleeping character
parentalGuidance.guidance: The Ugly Stepsister earns its R rating emphatically. This is body horror in the tradition of Cronenberg and Ducournau, wrapped in fairy tale aesthetics. The violence is not action-movie violence - it is intimate, surgical, and directed at women's bodies in the pursuit of beauty. Conservative parents should be aware that the film functions as a feminist critique of beauty culture, using extreme imagery to make its point. The body horror is the message: what women do to themselves to conform to beauty standards is presented as literal mutilation. The sexual content includes a scene of intercourse (not fully explicit) and a sexual act performed by the stepmother. The rotting corpse and tapeworm sequences will genuinely disturb viewers with weak stomachs. This is absolutely not a family film despite the fairy tale source material. For mature viewers 17 and up who can handle body horror, the film is well-crafted and thought-provoking, even if its politics are clearly feminist. Not suitable for children under any circumstances.

summary.overall:
Emilie Blichfeldt looked at Cinderella and asked the question nobody wanted answered: what would the ugly stepsister's story actually feel like if you told it honestly? The answer, it turns out, involves tapeworms, butcher knives, and more blood than a Dario Argento retrospective.

The Ugly Stepsister retells the Cinderella story from Elvira's perspective. Elvira is one of two daughters born to Rebekka, a widow who marries Otto, a widower with a beautiful daughter named Agnes. When Otto dies, leaving both families penniless, Rebekka hatches a plan: marry Elvira to Prince Julian at the upcoming royal ball. The problem is that Elvira is, by the film's fairy tale standards, ugly. Rebekka's solution is not encouragement or clever dressing. It is primitive cosmetic surgery, tapeworm diet pills, eyelash implants sewn directly into the eyelids, and eventually the butcher knife to the foot that Grimm fans know is coming.

Lea Myren delivers a remarkable performance as Elvira, carrying the film on a physical transformation that is simultaneously sympathetic and horrifying. Her Elvira begins the film as a dreamy girl with genuine affection for her new stepsister Agnes. Over the course of 109 minutes, she is systematically broken down by a beauty machine operated by her own mother, rebuilt into something the prince might notice, and then shattered when she discovers that the game was rigged from the start. Myren communicates volumes through physicality - the way Elvira holds herself changes as each procedure strips away another layer of her natural body.

Ane Dahl Torp is terrifying as Rebekka. This is a mother who has fully internalized the logic of a patriarchal marriage market and will carve her daughter's body to fit it. Torp plays the cruelty not as villainy but as pragmatism. Rebekka does not hate Elvira. She is simply doing what must be done to save the family from poverty. When she coldly tells Elvira she attempted to mutilate the wrong foot, it lands as the film's most chilling moment because Torp delivers the line with the tired patience of a parent correcting a child's homework.

Thea Sofie Loch Naess plays Agnes/Cinderella as neither saint nor villain. In Blichfeldt's reimagining, Agnes is haughty toward her stepfamily for their lower social status. She is beautiful, yes, but she is also a product of the same system. Her beauty is her only asset in a world that values nothing else in women. When Agnes is caught having sex with the stable boy Isak and is demoted to servant (becoming 'Cinderella'), the film reveals that even the beautiful girl is only one transgression away from losing everything.

The body horror is the point, not decoration. Every grotesque procedure Rebekka subjects Elvira to has a direct real-world analogue. The eyelash implants are extreme lash extensions. The tapeworm is a diet pill. The nose procedures are rhinoplasty. The foot cutting is the metaphorical (and in this case literal) reshaping of women's bodies to fit impossible standards. Blichfeldt uses the fairy tale setting to strip away the clinical sanitization that makes modern beauty culture palatable. What remains is the violence underneath - the fact that 'beauty routine' is a euphemism for controlled self-harm.

The film's feminist thesis is unmistakable. Every man in the story is either useless (Otto, who dies immediately), cruel (Prince Julian, a shallow womanizer who mocks Elvira's appearance), or incidental (Isak, the stable boy used and discarded). The women are trapped in a system where their only currency is appearance, and the older women (Rebekka, Sophie von Kronenberg at the finishing school) are the system's enforcers. This is feminist theory rendered as fairy tale - the idea that patriarchy is maintained not just by men but by women who have internalized its values and pass them to their daughters.

Where the film works best is in its final act. Elvira, broken and bleeding after crawling down a flight of stairs only to find that Agnes and the prince have already found each other, finally stops chasing the prize. Her younger sister Alma helps her expel the tapeworm in a sequence that is simultaneously the film's most disgusting and most cathartic moment. The sisters steal their mother's jewelry and ride away together - not toward a prince, not toward a happy ending as traditionally defined, but toward freedom from the beauty machine that nearly killed them both.

Where the film is less successful is in its treatment of Agnes/Cinderella. By making Agnes somewhat unsympathetic (haughty, classist), the film partially undermines its own thesis. If the point is that all women suffer under beauty standards, Agnes should be as much a victim as Elvira. Instead, Agnes gets the prince, the magical dress mended by silkworms, and the fairy godmother vision - the full Cinderella package - while Elvira gets mutilated. The film wants to have it both ways: Agnes is both a fellow victim of patriarchy and the lucky winner of the genetic lottery who gets everything Elvira cannot have.

The Oscar nomination for Best Makeup and Hairstyling is richly deserved. Anne Cathrine Sauerberg and Thomas Foldberg created prosthetic and practical effects work that makes every procedure feel sickeningly real. The eyelash sewing sequence reportedly made the makeup team themselves 'want to vomit on set.' The fact that this level of craft exists in service of a Norwegian debut filmmaker's $4.2 million budget is genuinely impressive.

Conservative audiences will find The Ugly Stepsister a mixed bag ideologically. The feminist framework is front and center - this is a film that explicitly critiques patriarchal beauty standards and presents female liberation from the marriage market as the happy ending. The prince is a shallow fool. The mother who enforces traditional femininity is the villain. The ending rejects marriage entirely in favor of sisterly independence.

But there is a quieter traditional thread here that the feminist framing does not entirely erase. The film condemns vanity with the ferocity of a medieval morality play. It treats the body as sacred - something that should not be cut, starved, or reshaped for someone else's approval. It celebrates sisterly love and loyalty over romantic love. And its villain is not tradition itself but the corruption of tradition into cruelty. Rebekka is not a traditional mother. She is a monster who uses the language of tradition to justify abuse. A conservative viewer could argue that the film actually demonstrates what happens when the market logic of transactional marriage replaces genuine love and virtue - that the problem is not patriarchy but the absence of authentic values.

That reading, however, is not what the filmmaker intended. Blichfeldt's stated purpose is feminist critique. The film she made is a feminist film. VirtueVigil scores what is on screen, and what is on screen is a carefully constructed argument that beauty standards are violence, the marriage market is a trap, and women's liberation lies in rejecting the entire system. It makes this argument with considerable skill, dark humor, and genuine emotional power. Whether you agree with the argument is another matter entirely.
summary.parentalGuidance: R-rated. Extensive body horror including cosmetic surgery, foot mutilation, tapeworm ingestion and expulsion, a rotting corpse, and sexual content. Not a family film despite the fairy tale source material. Recommended for mature viewers 17+ who can handle body horror. The film functions as a feminist critique of beauty standards using extreme imagery. Conservative parents should be aware of the explicit feminist framework.

creativeTeamProfiles.top: Emilie Blichfeldt (writer/director) is a Norwegian debut filmmaker who conceived the film from her own body image struggles and explicitly designed it as feminist commentary using body horror. Her primary influences are David Cronenberg, Julia Ducournau (Raw), Dario Argento, and Lucio Fulci. She is a progressive feminist filmmaker by stated intention. The production is Scandinavian indie cinema through Mer Film and Zentropa, far from the Hollywood machine.
creativeTeamProfiles.bottom: This is a debut feature from a film school graduate. The creative team has no prior track record to analyze for ideological patterns. The film's feminist perspective is the director's stated and demonstrated intention, not an inference.

tropeAudit.name: Beauty Standards as Patriarchal Violence
tropeAudit.description: The film's central thesis: beauty standards are a form of violence imposed on women by a patriarchal system. Every cosmetic procedure Elvira undergoes is presented as literal mutilation. The eyelash sewing, the tapeworm diet, the foot cutting - all are real-world beauty practices rendered as body horror to expose the violence underneath the euphemisms. This is the film's core message and drives every narrative and visual choice.

tropeAudit.name: Feminist Deconstruction of Fairy Tale
tropeAudit.description: The film deliberately inverts the Cinderella narrative to expose its patriarchal assumptions. By centering the 'ugly' stepsister instead of the beautiful heroine, and by making the prince a shallow fool rather than a worthy prize, Blichfeldt deconstructs the fairy tale's message that beauty equals virtue and marriage equals salvation. This is textbook feminist revisionism of a foundational cultural narrative.

tropeAudit.name: Female Liberation as Happy Ending
tropeAudit.description: The film ends not with a marriage but with Elvira and Alma stealing their mother's jewelry and riding away together, free from the beauty machine. The happy ending is explicitly defined as liberation from the marriage market and from the mother who enforced patriarchal standards. This replaces the fairy tale's traditional resolution (marriage to the prince) with a feminist one (sisterly independence).

tropeAudit.name: Male Characters as Useless or Villainous
tropeAudit.description: Every male character in the film is either pathetic or predatory. Otto dies immediately. Prince Julian is a shallow womanizer who mocks Elvira. Isak the stable boy is used for sex and discarded. Dr. Esthetique performs brutal procedures without concern. No man in the film offers genuine help, kindness, or partnership to any woman. This is a common pattern in feminist cinema but is somewhat mitigated by the fairy tale setting where all characters are archetypes.

tropeAudit.name: Internalized Misogyny Critique
tropeAudit.description: Rebekka, the mother/villain, is presented as a woman who has internalized patriarchal values and now enforces them on her daughters. Sophie von Kronenberg at the finishing school is another woman enforcing beauty standards. The film argues that patriarchy persists because women police each other. This is a standard feminist analysis of internalized misogyny.

tropeAudit.name: Anti-Vanity Morality
tropeAudit.description: The film condemns vanity with the ferocity of a medieval morality play. The pursuit of beauty is presented as literally destroying the body, the soul, and family bonds. Elvira's transformation is a cautionary tale about what happens when appearance is valued above substance. The tapeworm, the surgery, the foot mutilation - all are consequences of vanity. A preacher could preach this sermon, even if the filmmaker would not frame it that way.

tropeAudit.name: The Body as Sacred/Inviolable
tropeAudit.description: The horror of the film derives from the violation of Elvira's body. Every cut, every implant, every ingested parasite is presented as a violation of something that should be whole and untouched. The film's revulsion at body modification carries an implicitly conservative message: the natural body is good, and reshaping it for external approval is wrong. This aligns with traditional and religious views of the body as a sacred vessel.

tropeAudit.name: Sisterly Love and Loyalty
tropeAudit.description: The genuine emotional core of the film is the bond between Elvira and her younger sister Alma. Alma watches in horror as her mother destroys Elvira and hides her own puberty to avoid the same fate. In the end, it is Alma who helps Elvira expel the tapeworm and escape. Their sisterly loyalty is the film's only uncomplicated virtue - the one relationship not corrupted by the beauty machine.

tropeAudit.name: Rejection of Transactional Marriage
tropeAudit.description: While the film frames this as a feminist point, the condemnation of marriage-as-transaction can also be read traditionally. The film's villain is not marriage itself but the reduction of marriage to an economic arrangement where a woman's body is the currency. A traditional Christian would agree that this is a corruption of marriage. The film inadvertently argues for authentic, love-based marriage by showing the horror of the alternative.

tropeAudit.name: Maternal Villainy as Corruption of Motherhood
tropeAudit.description: Rebekka is one of the most disturbing movie mothers in recent memory. She sedates and mutilates her own daughter. The horror here is the corruption of the maternal instinct. The film presents this as monstrous precisely because motherhood should be protective and nurturing. A conservative can read this as a condemnation of what happens when a mother abandons her sacred role in favor of worldly pragmatism.
